item.content:encoded: Elfyn Evans ended years of heartache, and a quarter-of-a-century wait for Britain, by finally winning the World Rally Championship (WRC) title with Toyota after a dramatic season finale in Sardinia on Sunday. The Welshman had been championship runner-up five times in the last six years but emerged triumphant after a final Powerstage duel with teammate Oliver Solberg ended with the charging Swede crashing out two corners from the finish while on course to take the crown. Solberg, 25, ran wide and careered down a bank before getting the car back on the road. He still won the rally but lost the crucial bonus points on offer for the top five in the final stage. Evans, with co-driver Scott Martin at his side, became the first British world rally champion since Englishman Richard Burns in 2001 and only the third since Scottish driver Colin McRae became the nation's first in 1995. END OF AN ERA FOR RALLYING Sweden's Solberg, son of Norway's 2003 champion Petter, ended the season as runner-up. The final standings left Evans on 243 points, Solberg on 238 and Sami Pajari on 237 in what was also the end of an era for the sport with new regulations in force next year. "It hasn't sunk in. I was sure it was over. I didn't drive the best stage but threw everything at it but it wasn't clean. I feel for Oliver. He had an incredible weekend," said Evans, who completed his final run first and had to watch and wait to see whether he had done enough to take the title. "I don't really know what my reaction is, it's surreal with how it happened. It's a relief. It wouldn't be my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done," added the 37-year-old, who finished fifth in the gravel rally. Evans had started the rally -- the final round after Saudi Arabia's finale was cancelled due to conflict in the region -- 17 points clear of Finland's Pajari, also in a Toyota, and 21 clear of Solberg. The Swede took control of the rally on Saturday, knowing he had nothing to lose and all to gain, and started the final day 33.6 seconds clear of the field and the momentum swinging his way. That feeling was reinforced when Evans lost time changing a wheel on Sunday's penultimate stage, leaving the championship outcome hanging on the short final stage and the title going to which of the pair finished ahead of the other. Toyota had already won the manufacturers' championship.

item.title: Le président yéménite annonce une offensive d'envergure contre les Houthis
item.description: Le président yéménite, dont le gouvernement est soutenu par l'Arabie saoudite, a annoncé dimanche le lancement d'une vaste opération militaire contre les rebelles houthis pro-iraniens, visant à reprendre le contrôle des territoires qu'ils occupent.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Eman Abouhassira, Mohammed Ghobari
item.content:encoded: Le président yéménite, dont le gouvernement est soutenu par l'Arabie saoudite, a annoncé dimanche le lancement d'une vaste opération militaire contre les rebelles houthis pro-iraniens, visant à reprendre le contrôle des territoires qu'ils occupent. "Aujourd'hui, j'annonce le lancement d'opérations militaires visant à reprendre le reste du territoire de la République et à étendre l'autorité de l'Etat et de ses institutions à l'ensemble du territoire national", a déclaré Rachad al Alimi dans une allocution télévisée. Des responsables régionaux et occidentaux ont dit il y a quelques jours à Reuters que l'Arabie saoudite et ses alliés yéménites prévoyaient cette offensive contre les Houthis, les Saoudiens s'occupant des combats aériens et les forces yéménites combattant au sol. De leur côté, les Houthis ont annoncé ce dimanche avoir lancé des drones et des missiles balistiques sur des sites d'Aramco, la compagnie pétrolière nationale de l'Arabie saoudite, dans les régions de Ryad et de Khurais. Ils ont précisé que ces attaques, qui ont provoqué de gigantesques incendies, étaient des représailles contre, selon eux, 50 frappes menées contre le Yemen au cours des 12 dernières heures par la coalition dirigée par l'Arabie saoudite. Ryad n'a pas confirmé à ce stade les attaques revendiquées par les Houthis. Selon Rachad al Alimi, la décision de lancer cette contre-offensive a été prise après l'épuisement de toutes les possibilités de désescalade, la président yéménite accusant les Houthis d'avoir répondu aux efforts visant à apaiser le conflit par une mobilisation accrue et une escalade. "Notre position aujourd'hui est d'assumer la responsabilité nationale de faire face aux Houthis, après que toutes les possibilités de désescalade ont été épuisées", a-t-il déclaré. Rachad al Alimi a dit avoir ordonné aux forces armées, aux forces de sécurité et à toutes les formations militaires de commencer à exécuter les missions qui leur ont été confiées, conformément aux plans approuvés. L'IMPORTANCE DE TAÏZ, TROISIÈME VILLE DU PAYS La reprise du conflit au Yemen a provoqué le déplacement de dizaines de milliers de personnes et pourrait redessiner le paysage politique, avec des répercussions sur les voies maritimes de la mer Rouge et le [USN:L8N4530M9 TEXT:"détroit de Bab el-Mandeb"], autre axe vital pour le transport maritime mondial d'hydrocarbures. Les Houthis, qui se sont emparés en septembre 2014 de la capitale yéménite Sanaa, résultat d'un complexe jeu d'alliances sur fond de guerre civile, résistent depuis plus de dix ans à une coalition mise sur pied par l'Arabie saoudite, en s'appuyant sur un arsenal de drones et missiles balistiques constitué avec l'aide de Téhéran. Une trêve conclue sous l'égide des Nations unies entre les parties belligérantes en 2022 a globalement tenu jusqu'à cette année, quand les Houthis ont commencé à lancer des attaques contre le transport maritime et les infrastructures pétrolières saoudiennes, en réaction à l'attaque lancée le 28 février par les Etats-Unis et Israël contre l'Iran. Les Houthis, qui contrôlent les zones les plus peuplées du Yémen et une grande partie du nord du pays dont la capitale Sanaa, ont lancé plusieurs attaques contre l'Arabie saoudite - alliée des Etats-Unis - et en mer Rouge depuis leur annonce en juillet dernier d'un blocus maritime des ports saoudiens. Malgré les préparatifs d'une contre-offensive, les Houthis ont jusqu'à présent conservé l'initiative sur le terrain, et ce plusieurs semaines après s'être emparés du détroit de Bab el-Mandeb lors d’une offensive éclair le long de la côte. Ce détroit, la sortie sud de la mer Rouge, est une voie maritime clé entre la Méditerranée et l'Asie et elle a pris encore plus d'importance, depuis le début de la guerre déclenchée le 28 février contre l'Iran, en tant qu'alternative au détroit d'Ormuz, puisque ce dernier a de fait été fermé par Téhéran. Au cours des dernières 48 heures, les Houthis ont réalisé des avancées face aux forces gouvernementales et locales sur des collines stratégiques près de Taïz, dans le sud-ouest du Yémen, ont dit des sources militaires. Les Houthis ont ainsi progressé sur la dernière route reliant la ville à Aden, où est basé le gouvernement yéménite soutenu par l'Arabie saoudite. La prise de contrôle par les Houthis de la route Taïz-Aden entraînerait un siège de fait de Taïz, troisième plus grande ville du Yémen, où vivent des centaines de milliers de civils et où sont également stationnés des milliers de soldats des forces gouvernementales. La ville revêt une importance qui ne tient pas uniquement à sa position stratégique: le président yéménite Rachad al Alimi est originaire de cette région et un siège de Taïz exacerberait une situation humanitaire déjà désastreuse dans le pays. La [USN:L6N45O0MZ TEXT:"famine"] au Yémen s'aggrave, avec un nombre record d'habitants incapables de subvenir à leurs besoins alimentaires, alors que le conflit avec l'Arabie Saoudite s'intensifie, a déclaré vendredi le Programme alimentaire mondial (PAM).

item.title: Yemeni government launches offensive to seize all areas from Iran-backed Houthis
item.description: Despite the preparations for a counteroffensive, the Houthis have maintained the initiative on the ground, weeks after seizing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in a lightning offensive that saw government forces collapse.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Ghobari, Timour Azhari, Eman Abouhassira
item.content:encoded: Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government said on Sunday it was launching a major military campaign to recapture all areas of the country controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis . The government’s armed forces would press the offensive “until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia,” Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address. A military spokesman later called on the Houthis to lay down their weapons. The Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, have held Yemen’s capital Sanaa and vast parts of the northwest, where most of the population live, since 2014. They have so far withstood a series of attacks over the years by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and their Western allies, and have updated their weaponry with the help of Iran. The movement launched a surprise offensive last month which captured the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait and some 150 km (90 miles) of coast on the Red Sea in a matter of weeks, giving the Houthis new leverage over the international shipping route. That advance also opened a new front in the wider US-Israeli war launched in February against Iran, to which Tehran’s responses included choking oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz , to the other side of the Arabian Peninsula. HOUTHIS SAY THEY STRUCK SAUDI ARABIA As the Yemeni government, known as the Presidential Leadership Council, made its announcement, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia. They claimed the attacks caused major fires and were in response to what they said were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia. Alimi said the decision to launch the counteroffensive came after all chances of de-escalating the conflict had been exhausted. He thanked Saudi Arabia for its support and called on Yemen's regional allies and international partners to support PLC forces and institutions. Regional and western officials had told Reuters earlier this week that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to [USN:L8N45M1W0 TEXT:"launch an assault"] on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground. NEW FRONT IN MIDEAST WAR The US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh's operations in Yemen, while some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations told Reuters. The United States’ war on Iran has decimated a layer of Iranian military and political leadership, but has also entangled Washington in a new engagement in the Middle East and depleted crucial military hardware. Yemen has been mired in conflict for years, with an array of local armed groups and factions backed by competing regional and international actors. After a popular uprising that was part of the Arab Spring movements in 2011, the Houthis, an armed group of Zaidi Shi’ite Muslims, captured Sanaa. The Saudi-backed PLC, which is also recognised by the United Nations, has since the Houthi takeover controlled the south and east of the country, based in the former South Yemen capital of Aden. Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the PLC, but failed to defeat the Houthis. A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war. HOUTHIS ON FRONT FOOT The Houthis have maintained the initiative on the ground since seizing control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in their lightning offensive last month that saw government forces collapse. Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. In the last 48 hours, the Houthis have also made gains against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Yemen's Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden on the southern coast. Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen's third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians and where thousands of government forces are also stationed. The city is important not just for its strategic location; Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the country. Three in four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.

item.title: Australia probes flydubai co-pilot's links to the country, police say
item.description: The co-pilot, identified as an Omani, studied at a university in Melbourne, sources said.
item.dc:creator: Praveen Menon, Alexander Cornwell
item.content:encoded: A multi-agency Australian counterterrorism unit is investigating links to Australia of the co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, who stabbed his captain and then [USN:L1N45P01E TEXT:"attempted to hijack"] the plane, a police spokesperson said on Sunday. The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team – which comprises federal police, Victorian state police and the ASIO intelligence agency – was "investigating the man's links to Australia," the Australian Federal Police spokesperson said. Two sources briefed on the investigation said the co-pilot studied at a university in Melbourne, the capital of the Australian state of Victoria. A third source said he studied at RMIT University around a decade ago. RMIT declined to comment. The co-pilot of the [USN:L1N45P02M TEXT:"flydubai flight FZ1073"], which was bound for Israel from Dubai on Wednesday, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, calling the incident a "[USN:S8N43T02Z TEXT:"terrorist attack"]". Flight FZ1073 would have felt like a [USN:L4N45Q00M TEXT:""vertical roller coaster""], when it plunged 16,000 feet in about 30 seconds before being levelled out and landing safely, according to an aviation instructor who recreated the descent in a flight simulator for Reuters. CO-PILOT IN CUSTODY IN UAE Two sources have said the co-pilot is an Omani national named Hamam Al-Hamami. Israeli officials have not named the co-pilot but said that he is from Oman. UAE authorities and flydubai have not publicly disclosed the co-pilot's identity. Reuters could not independently reach Al-Hamami, who is in UAE custody, for comment. The UAE has not announced any formal charges against him and it is not known if he has appointed legal counsel. Oman has not commented on the incident. Disaster on board flight FZ1073 was averted after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had attacked the captain in what Israeli officials said was an attempt to crash the plane carrying more than 170 passengers and crew. The UAE public prosecutor has said the co-pilot had attempted to take control of the plane. RADICAL MOSQUES AND EXTREMIST WEBSITES Most of the passengers on board were Israeli nationals. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities and later transferred to the UAE on Thursday. The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Al-Hamami had allegedly visited what it described as radical mosques and extremist websites while in Australia, citing two people familiar with the investigation. Australian intelligence services held a file on the individual, according to the Financial Times. Reuters could not immediately verify the FT report. The government of Australia did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside normal business hours. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot had undergone radical [USN:L6N45N0GW TEXT:"Islamist indoctrination"] and was clearly suicidal, although he has not said when or where that indoctrination allegedly occurred. On Sunday he instructed the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to "conduct a thorough review of all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel". Israel does not have official diplomatic relations with Oman, and Netanyahu has also said pilots from such countries were not permitted to operate flights to Israel. It is not clear how the co-pilot came to be assigned to the flight to Tel Aviv.

item.title: Protests intensify in India over demands for election chief to quit
item.description: Thousands of youth protesters and opposition supporters rallied in Delhi and Mumbai on Sunday to demand the resignation of India's election commission chief over changes to voter rolls, as police detained some demonstrators for a third day.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Sharma
item.content:encoded: Thousands of youth protesters and opposition supporters rallied in Delhi and Mumbai on Sunday to demand the resignation of India's election commission chief over changes to voter rolls, as police detained some demonstrators for a third day. Opposition leaders Raj Thackeray and Uddhav Thackeray led protests in Mumbai, calling for the revisions to be scrapped and for Election Commission Chief [USN:L4N45K0DB TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar"] to step down. The protesters say the changes benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a charge denied by the Election Commission and the BJP. In the capital, New Delhi, protesters started gathering in the early evening and some were detained by police, according to a Reuters witness. Some demonstrators breached police barricades and surrounded vehicles carrying detained demonstrators, climbing onto them and laying on the road to block their path, the witness added. "Police dragged me by my hair," said Aahna Singh, an activist and political science student at Jawaharlal Nehru University who was protesting. "The police are resorting to brutality." Delhi Police did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. Police in the capital have prevented protesters from [USN:L4N45P01A TEXT:"assembling"] over the last two days, detaining dozens of them and transporting them away by bus. Some of the detainees were released later on Friday and Saturday, but police registered cases against some on charges of violating orders banning mass gatherings in the centre of the capital. PROTESTERS SAY VOTER ROLL CHANGES EXCLUDE MILLIONS The protesters say the nationwide voter-roll revision exercise launched last year has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters by removing them from electoral rolls in a way that will benefit Modi's party. "I just want to tell the ruling party this much... We are angry about how you are wielding that power. It's the people of this country who should decide who sits in power and who sits in opposition, not the Election Commission," the opposition leader Raj Thackeray said. The Election Commission says the exercise is designed to remove duplicate, deceased, or ineligible entries and maintain electoral integrity. On Friday, it directed its officials to register eligible voters inadvertently omitted from electoral rolls. Kumar has not publicly responded to the demands for his resignation or commented on the protests, which look set to continue over the next few days due to more planned rallies. An alliance of India's opposition parties plans to launch protests to "[USN:L6N45M0NH TEXT:"save democracy"]" with a march to the Election Commission office on Tuesday. The Gen Z Cockroach Janta Party has announced plans for a major rally in Delhi on October 10. The demonstrations represent the latest in a series of youth-led challenges to Modi's government — unprecedented in his 12 years in power. In July, student protests forced the ouster of the federal education minister following a leak of question papers for a national medical college entrance examination, marking the worst political crisis of Modi's third term in office. (This story has been corrected to change the day of the opposition march to Tuesday, not Monday, in the third bullet point and paragraph 14.)

item.title: Votação chega ao fim em eleição polarizada entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro
item.description: As quase 500 mil seções eleitorais espalhadas pelo Brasil começaram a ser fechadas às 17h deste domingo, dando início à expectativa para a divulgação do resultado em uma disputa pela Presidência da República acirrada e polarizada entre o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Simões
item.content:encoded: As quase 500 mil seções eleitorais espalhadas pelo Brasil começaram a ser fechadas às 17h deste domingo, dando início à expectativa para a divulgação do resultado em uma disputa pela Presidência da República acirrada e polarizada entre o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). Marcada por polêmicas envolvendo desde o Judiciário até a padroeira do Brasil, passando por denúncias generalizadas de corrupção e temores de interferência externa, a campanha eleitoral para presidente chegou ao primeiro turno com a disputa totalmente em aberto entre os dois principais candidatos. Lula e Flávio votaram no começo da manhã e manifestaram confiança na vitória. Ao votar em uma escola em São Bernardo do Campo (SP), Lula fez um apelo para que os eleitores com mais de 70 anos comparecessem às urnas e reafirmou que o que estava em jogo nas eleições era a escolha entre o "fortalecimento do regime democrático e a barbárie". Flávio Bolsonaro votou em uma escola em Vila Isabel, no Rio de Janeiro, pouco após a abertura das urnas, e disse que esperava vencer já no primeiro turno. "As nossas pesquisas internas mostram que a gente ultrapassou no primeiro turno já faz algum tempo", declarou. "Espero que seja suficiente para dar vitória no primeiro turno." As pesquisas de intenção de voto divulgadas no sábado, no entanto, apontam para uma nova rodada de votação, que aconteceria em 25 de outubro. Para a eleição acabar neste domingo, é preciso que um dos candidatos conquiste mais de 50% dos votos válidos, quando são desconsiderados os votos brancos e nulos. Levantamentos do Datafolha e da Quaest colocaram Lula e Flávio em empate técnico no primeiro turno nos votos válidos, com vantagem numérica do atual presidente de 3 pontos na primeira e de 1 ponto na segunda. Uma outra pesquisa, do MDA, colocou Lula com 47,8% dos votos válidos contra 42,1% de Flávio. O presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), Kassio Nunes Marques, afirmou confiar em um processo tranquilo de votação: "Amanhecemos o dia hoje com a segurança de que as eleições vão transcorrer na maior normalidade", disse, ao votar em Brasília no início da manhã. Os mais de 158,7 milhões de brasileiros aptos a votar puderam ir às seções eleitorais ao longo do dia -- as urnas abriram às 8h e fecharam às 17h pelo horário de Brasília -- após meses de embates muitas vezes em nível pessoal de cada lado, em que as propostas para governar o país pelos próximos quatro anos não foram protagonistas. A campanha chegou ao fim sem que Lula e Flávio tenham se enfrentado diretamente. No debate da TV Bandeirantes, ambos decidiram não ir, deixando os púlpitos vazios com seus nomes para serem criticados por Augusto Cury (Avante), Renan Santos (Missão) e Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), que estavam presentes. Romeu Zema (Novo) completa a lista dos outros candidatos cujos partidos têm representação no Congresso, mas cujas intenções de voto jamais se aproximaram da dos dois líderes. Já o debate da TV Globo, que tradicionalmente encerra as campanhas, acabou sendo [USN:L1N45N18V TEXT:"cancelado"] após uma série de decisões judiciais e da desistência de última hora de Flávio, filho mais velho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro -- que está atualmente em prisão domiciliar após ser condenado por tentativa de golpe de Estado. Lula havia dito dias antes que não compareceria. Nunes Marques disse esperar que candidatos acionem a Justiça com questionamentos relacionados às eleições, mas frisou, em entrevista coletiva nesta tarde, que a votação está transcorrendo com normalidade e transparência. Segundo ele, as urnas estão funcionando normalmente e não houve necessidade de votação manual em nenhum ponto do país. TEMOR DE INTERFERÊNCIA A eleição também ocorre em meio a renovados temores sobre uma possível interferência estrangeira na eleição presidencial brasileira. A Reuters [USN:L6N45M0VR TEXT:"revelou"] na última semana que autoridades francesas e alemãs ouviram de membros da Agência Brasileira de Inteligência (Abin) que já estariam acontecendo tentativas de interferência dos Estados Unidos e da Rússia no pleito. O diretor-geral da Polícia Federal, Andrei Rodrigues, afirmou neste domingo que a corporação já abriu investigação para apurar suposto esquema de financiamento de uma agenda de extrema-direita no Brasil pelo governo norte-americano de Donald Trump que teria entre os objetivos interferir nas eleições brasileiras. A investigação foi solicitada pela Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) na quinta-feira e teve como base reportagem publicada no jornal inglês The Guardian, segundo a qual o Departamento de Estado norte-americano teria destinado US$1 milhão de um fundo ligado aos direitos humanos e à democracia para um programa chamado "Combate ao Lawfare e à Censura no Brasil". Nunes Marques enfatizou, no entanto, que o TSE não identificou nenhum indicativo de interferência estrangeira nas eleições. “Equipes que monitoram riscos internacionais não apontam qualquer tipo de risco”, afirmou. Na última quinta-feira, a embaixada dos EUA no Brasil [USN:L6N45O0XD TEXT:"anunciou"] a suspensão dos serviços consulares a partir da sexta-feira, alegando preocupações não especificadas de segurança. Além disso, a embaixada pediu aos seus funcionários que trabalhassem de casa na sexta após uma ameaça. A embaixadora da Austrália também anunciou o fechamento da representação diplomática do país em Brasília citando o alerta norte-americano. A medida foi criticada pelo presidente do PT, Edinho Silva, que viu tentativa do governo do presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, de influenciar a opinião pública brasileira. Neste domingo, no entanto, Nunes Marques ponderou que a iniciativa seria usual no caso de eleições acirradas, e citou que teria acontecido o fechamento de embaixadas também durante o último pleito na Colômbia. A relação com os EUA e com Trump foi um dos principais marcadores da diferença entre Lula e Flávio. Enquanto o presidente alertou o homólogo norte-americano publicamente a não interferir no Brasil, o senador procurou mostrar proximidade com Trump, inclusive visitando-o na Casa Branca. "É uma relação tensa porque o Brasil não quer se ver dentro da zona de influência dos EUA. Tradicionalmente a nossa diplomacia é independente. O Lula acredita que, pela boa relação com a China, especialmente a comercial, que manter essa independência é fundamental", disse Leonardo Barreto, cofundador da Think Policy. "O Flávio tenta fazer dos EUA uma espécie de fiador das eleições. A família Bolsonaro acredita que as eleições não são feitas em condições de liberdade. Desconfiança em relação a urna, meios de comunicação, administração do Judiciário. Buscam no apoio dos americanos uma espécie de pressão para garantir o mínimo de neutralidade das autoridades brasileiras, percebem nos americanos uma espécie de seguro", acrescentou. BETS, STF E PADROEIRA Em meio a denúncias de corrupção como as do Banco Master e o escândalo do INSS, que atingiram tanto Flávio quanto o filho mais velho de Lula, além de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), a campanha também foi marcada pelo apelo do senador à imagem de seu pai, ao mesmo tempo em que buscava se mostrar mais moderado do que o ex-presidente, enquanto Lula seguiu batendo na tecla dos seus três mandatos na Presidência e lançando mão de medidas populares às vésperas do pleito. Entre elas, o governo anunciou o reajuste de 15% nos benefícios do Bolsa Família, a edição de uma medida provisória para proibir casas de apostas online e o anúncio da intenção de distribuir gratuitamente pelo Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) as chamadas canetas emagrecedoras, três medidas aprovadas pelo eleitorado, segundo as pesquisas de opinião. Mas a polêmica que marcou a reta final da campanha ficou por conta de rumores de que Flávio retiraria de Nossa Senhora Aparecida o título de padroeira do Brasil, o que foi negado com veemência pelo senador. Flávio classificou os boatos de "fake news", enquanto Lula disse que, enquanto for presidente, ninguém irá "avacalhar" com Nossa Senhora. Além do presidente, os eleitores também escolherão neste domingo os governadores dos 26 Estados e do Distrito Federal, além de 54 dos 81 senadores e dos 513 deputados e dos integrantes das Assembleias Legislativas de 26 Estados e da Câmara Distrital do Distrito Federal. A eleição para o Senado estará sob o foco, em um momento de pressão sobre ministros do STF, que podem sofrer impeachment pelos integrantes da Casa, e em um momento em que estão [USN:L6N45N0ZL TEXT:"vagas"] funções em órgãos reguladores, como o Banco Central, cujos nomes precisam ser aprovados pelos senadores.

item.title: Brazil's Bolsonaro takes early lead as results trickle in for high-stakes election
item.description: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, is seeking a fourth term as president while Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, hopes to return his father's right-wing movement to power.
item.dc:creator: Brendan O'Boyle, Luciana Magalhaes, Rodrigo Viga Gaier
item.content:encoded: Senator Flavio Bolsonaro took an early lead as Brazil began reporting results on Sunday afternoon in the first round of a tight presidential election, following a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling. The field of 13 candidates has been led by two clear frontrunners — leftist [USN:L6N459162 TEXT:"President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva"], 80, who is seeking a fourth term, and Flavio, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who hopes to return his father's right-wing movement to power. With about 32% of votes reported, Flavio led Lula with 50.74% of the votes to the president's 41.14%. Early results showed southern states that lean to Bolsonaro reporting faster, while votes from Lula's northeast stronghold are tallied slower. If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes, the top two will face off on October 25. Surveys show Lula and Flavio polling roughly even in a likely runoff. A victory for the senator would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's reelection could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security. Despite growing worries over Brazil's public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign offered [USN:L1N4580UE TEXT:"meager policy debate"], as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates. UNDECIDED VOTERS While polls right up until Saturday showed Lula would likely lead the first round but not avoid a runoff, Flavio told journalists in Rio de Janeiro he was confident he could win the presidency in the first round, citing voters' frustration with his chief opponent. Flavio was counting on "a protest vote from people who would otherwise vote for another candidate but are opposed to Lula," he said. "I hope it’s enough to secure a victory in the first round." Thaise Lima, a 41-year-old lawyer on her way to vote in Sao Paulo, said her main goal was to get Lula's Workers' Party out of office. "I don't think Flavio is the best candidate, but I might decide to vote for him in the next few minutes," she said, adding that she wished psychiatrist and author Augusto Cury were a more viable candidate. Fernando Tempel, 49, a management consultant, told Reuters he was voting for Flavio despite initially planning to vote for Romeu Zema, the former governor of Minas Gerais state. OUTSIDE INTERFERENCE On the other hand, Lula's allies have warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognize election results if he wins, pointing to an aborted effort to [USN:L6N43R03C TEXT:"send US officials to Brazil"]. "What is at stake is the future of Brazil," Lula said after voting in Sao Bernardo do Campo, in Sao Paulo state. Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted Senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly. "I'm a little worried about everything that's been happening recently, including internationally. I feel this election has had a lot of outside influence, more than in previous elections," said Cristiano, 34, a doctor in Brasilia who voted for Lula and preferred to withhold his surname. "We are confident in our President Lula, who will fight for national sovereignty," said Pedro Palacio, 45, who was voting in Brasilia alongside his wife, Andreia, and their two sons and two dogs, all of whom wore outfits supporting the president. As of Sunday afternoon, the election was proceeding normally, Brazil's electoral court chief Kassio Nunes Marques said in a press conference. “Teams monitoring international risks have not identified any risks whatsoever," he said. Reuters reported on Wednesday that Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and German delegation on [USN:L1N45E08V TEXT:"alleged US and Russian interference"] before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil's affairs. ECONOMIC HEADWINDS Despite [USN:L1N44111S TEXT:"falling inequality"] and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity. Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families. Rising spending and public debt above 82% of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil's next president will need to address. The government lowered its [USN:L1N45E0QC TEXT:"economic growth forecasts"] for this year and next to 2.0% and 2.3% respectively. "I voted for Brazil to start growing again," said Marciano de Souza e Silva, a 52-year-old public servant in Brasilia and former Lula voter who moved right, voting for Jair Bolsonaro in 2018 and 2022 and Flavio on Sunday. "The best social program is one that encourages people to start businesses, to actually produce real wealth," he said. SCANDAL-PLAGUED CAMPAIGNS Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed much of Brazil's political class and renewed public anger over corruption. Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier this year and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme. The investigation has probed the banker's ties to figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Flavio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to the case by the federal police. The candidate has denied any wrongdoing, although he confirmed raising millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father. The banker's connections to Moraes, widely perceived as a Lula ally, [USN:L6N44U1B6 TEXT:"plunged the court into crisis"] a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the president. Moraes has said the case against him is politically motivated for his role in the [USN:L1N45711X TEXT:"conviction of the elder Bolsonaro"]. On Sunday, voters will also elect all 513 lower house members and two-thirds of the Senate, where some lawmakers have pushed to impeach Moraes. Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment of former President Dilma Rousseff, a Lula ally, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races.

item.title: Two dead in flooding in Spain's Catalonia region
item.description: Two people have died and another was missing after heavy rains and flooding in Spain's Catalonia region, authorities said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Two people have died and another was missing after heavy rains and flooding in Spain's Catalonia region, authorities said on Sunday. Catalan leader Salvador Illa confirmed the death of a man after a wall collapsed in Tordera, a town to the north of Barcelona, in a message on his social media account on Sunday. Another person died in Montornès del Vallès, firefighters said on Sunday, while emergency services were searching for a missing person in Pineda de Mar, a town 52 km (32 miles) to the north of Barcelona. Catalan authorities issued a red alert warning and urged people to stay inside from 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) on Saturday until Sunday at 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) because a "mini-hurricane" could hit the northeastern region, with more heavy rain forecast. Homes were flooded and cars left submerged in Bellvitge and Cornella near Barcelona after torrential rain on Saturday. Ducks swam in huge puddles that formed on motorways in Barcelona. Sarai Sarroca, director of regional weather service Meteocat, said on Saturday that the core of an exceptional weather system was over the Mediterranean and a "mini-hurricane" could move over land in Catalonia. Flights were cancelled or delayed at Barcelona airport, La Vanguardia newspaper reported on Saturday. All local trains were disrupted by the deluge. Shops shut early, football matches were called off and a performance of Verdi's Aida at Barcelona's Liceu opera house was cancelled.

item.title: Éthiopie-La capitale du Tigré sous contrôle des forces gouvernementales
item.description: Les forces gouvernementales éthiopiennes et les milices alliées ont repris le contrôle de la capitale du Tigré, ont-elles déclaré dimanche, infligeant ainsi un revers majeur à l'alliance d'opposition qui gouverne cette région du nord.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les forces gouvernementales éthiopiennes et les milices alliées ont repris le contrôle de la capitale du Tigré, ont-elles déclaré dimanche, infligeant ainsi un revers majeur à l'alliance d'opposition qui gouverne cette région du nord. Les Forces de paix du Tigré, une milice pro-gouvernementale dit dans un message publié sur Facebook que ses combattants avaient pris le contrôle de Mekelle, la capitale du Tigré. Une source proche de la milice avait auparavant dit à Reuters qu'elle était entrée dans le centre-ville samedi après-midi, suivie par l'armée éthiopienne. Le Front populaire de libération du Tigré (TPLF), qui dirige l'alliance d'opposition, a dit de son côté dans un communiqué publié sur Facebook qu'il s'était retiré de Mekelle, et que le gouvernement régional serait "temporairement transféré hors de Mekelle et opérerait depuis un autre endroit". Une source humanitaire et un habitant de Mekelle, sous couvert d'anonymat, ont confirmé que la ville était désormais aux mains des forces gouvernementales. Le cabinet du Premier ministre Abiy Ahmed n'a pas répondu dans l'immédiat à une demande de commentaire. La prise de Mekelle par les forces pro-gouvernementales constitue une importante perte pour l'alliance d'opposition dirigée par le TPLF, qui avait lancé une vaste [USN:L8N45F0T4 TEXT:"offensive"] le 23 septembre contre l'armée éthiopienne. Les forces fédérales éthiopiennes et les combattants alliés ont lancé une contre-offensive rapide dans le Tigré, mais selon les analystes, ces combats — qui constituent la pire escalade depuis la guerre civile de 2020-2022 — risquent de dégénérer en un conflit régional plus vaste. Le gouvernement fédéral d'Addis-Abeba a rompu ses relations diplomatiques avec l'Érythrée la semaine dernière, l'accusant de soutenir l'alliance rebelle aux côtés du Soudan et de l'Égypte. Les trois pays rejettent ces accusations.

item.title: Government forces seize capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region from rebels
item.description: Pro-government forces have regained control of the capital of Tigray, they said on Sunday, dealing a major setback to the opposition alliance that rules the northern Ethiopian region.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Pro-government forces have regained control of the capital of Tigray, they said on Sunday, dealing a major setback to the opposition alliance that rules the northern Ethiopian region. The Tigray Peace Forces, a pro-government militia, said in a post on Facebook that its fighters controlled Mekelle. A source close to the militia had earlier told Reuters it entered the centre of the city on Saturday afternoon, followed by the Ethiopian military. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which leads the opposition alliance, said in a statement it had retreated from the capital and that the regional government would be "temporarily moved out of Mekelle and operate from somewhere else". A humanitarian source and a Mekelle resident, who asked not to be named, confirmed the city was in the hands of government forces and their allies. LOSS OF MEKELLE A MAJOR BLOW FOR TPLF The taking of Mekelle by pro-government forces is a major loss for the opposition alliance led by the TPLF, which [USN:L6N45G0U0 TEXT:"launched a big offensive"] on September 23 against the Ethiopian military. Ethiopian federal forces have made a quick counterattack into Tigray, but analysts say the fighting — the worst escalation since a 2020-2022 civil war — threatens to escalate into a wider regional conflict. The federal government in Addis Ababa severed diplomatic ties with Eritrea last week, accusing it of supporting the rebel alliance alongside Sudan and Egypt. Egypt's foreign minister denied backing the TPLF and its allies. "I have to be very clear, we are not party to the domestic crisis facing Ethiopia now. It has nothing to do with us," Badr Abdelatty told Reuters on Sunday. Eritrea and Sudan also deny helping the rebels. Abdelatty was speaking ahead of a meeting between Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and his Eritrean and Somali counterparts in Egypt on Sunday. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the head of Sudan’s army, was also due to attend the talks. Egypt and Ethiopia, two of Africa’s most populous countries, have been at loggerheads for years over Ethiopia’s construction of a major dam on the Nile River, which Egypt views as a threat to its water security. “It is an existential issue. It’s life or death for 110 million people,” Abdelatty said.

item.title: Saudi Arabia quietly shelving NEOM Stadium, one of 2034 World Cup venues
item.description: It was meant to be one of the most ambitious venues for the 2034 FIFA World Cup.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia is quietly shelving plans to build one of its most ambitious stadiums for the 2034 FIFA World Cup, two sources familiar with the matter said, after delays and downscaling of the futuristic development housing it. The NEOM Stadium was billed as an elevated arena in a glitzy 100-mile (160-km) steel and glass structure known as The Line, in turn part of the broader development known as NEOM. NEOM was introduced about a decade ago as a centrepiece of de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030, an ambitious plan to diversify the economy and cut reliance on oil. Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of NEOM's owner the Public Investment Fund, confirmed in April that The Line was [USN:S8N40J01E TEXT:"no longer a priority"], and said it was not vital before 2030, the original delivery target for its first phase. He denied any projects had been cancelled. However, according to two sources, plans to build the NEOM Stadium have now been shelved indefinitely. NEOM and the Saudi government media office did not reply to requests for comment, while Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Sports redirected questions to the World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority. The Authority said "substantial delivery" of construction milestones for the event was already taking place, but did not address questions around the NEOM Stadium and costs. It shared images of some of the other stadiums under construction. RIYADH DEVELOPING 15 VENUES FOR 2034 WORLD CUP The 2034 World Cup is seen as a marquee event for Saudi Arabia, which under the Vision 2030 programme has invested heavily in sports via wealth fund PIF. The tournament will be the first time a single nation hosts the expanded 48-team format. Riyadh is working to build or renovate 15 venues across five cities, as well as dozens of training facilities. MEED Projects, a Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform whose team of analysts tracks tenders and projects in the region, puts the total value of the projects at $22.7 billion in data shared with Reuters. According to MEED, NEOM's stadium is expected to cost $2.5 billion. It lists the projected 46,000-seat stadium in its data as "on hold". The stadium has no listed completion date, according to the data, which describes the remaining stadiums and facilities as in various stages of development, with completion expected between 2026 and 2033. Saudi Arabia is under increasing pressure from the Iran war, which has led to heavy disruptions to energy shipments and damage to critical infrastructure, with the kingdom facing attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis. Last week, the Ministry of Finance said it [USN:L1N45M0WE TEXT:"expected"] a fiscal deficit this year wider than previously projected and a real GDP contraction of 3.6% following a drop in oil activities. PIVOT FROM GIGA-PROJECTS The geographic distribution of the stadiums adds to the challenge of delivering the projects, a third source said. That could further be compounded by some projects set to host stadiums being delayed or downsized, such as The Line or Riyadh's New Murabba development, the source added. In January Reuters [USN:L1N3YR0WK TEXT:"reported"] that Saudi Arabia has suspended construction of The Mukaab, a colossal cube-shaped skyscraper at the centre of the New Murabba. Reuters also reported last year that the PIF was pivoting from its focus on costly giga-projects to endeavours with more immediate financial returns, a strategy [USN:L1N40Y0DC TEXT:"later articulated"] by Saudi officials. Still, other projects for the World Cup are progressing. The [USN:L6N43I0ZY TEXT:"Aramco Stadium"] in the eastern city of Al Khobar is set to be completed by the end of this year and host its first game in January, for which tickets are on sale. Work on other planned stadiums is going ahead, a fourth source said.

item.title: Latvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after election win
item.description: Andris Kulbergs has promised to improve governance and reduce public spending.
item.dc:creator: Andrius Sytas
item.content:encoded: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his centrist United List secured the biggest [USN:L8N45O1BP TEXT:"parliamentary election"] victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991. With 97% of ballots counted after Saturday's election in the NATO and European Union country bordering Russia, United List was on 35.3%, enough for 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament. A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray [USN:L8N41K055 TEXT:"Ukrainian military drones"] flew undetected into Latvia. Latvia's economy has underperformed its Baltic neighbours for more than a decade and Kulbergs has vowed to improve governance, cut red tape and reduce public spending, political scientist Roberts Kits said. "Kulbergs played on being a get-things-done type of guy and has persuaded the voters that he can do things differently, bring some fresh energy," he said. "This means the responsibility is huge. People expect him to deliver, but the question remains whether he has the team to do it." United List appeared able to secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives, Kits said. "(Kulbergs) is smart, let's hope that something will be better, that he will change what can be changed", Aina Sturmane, 78, a pensioner, told Reuters in Riga on Sunday. No Latvian government has survived a full term, and Kulbergs will face an uphill battle holding together the United List, a loose alliance of small parties and independents, said political scientist Janis Ikstens. PM PLEDGES TO MAINTAIN HARD LINE ON RUSSIA Kulbergs pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line towards Moscow. "Any economic ties with Russia makes us weak. Yes, it can bring some extra money, but it's a weakness Russia might exploit," he told reporters at his party's headquarters on election night as supporters celebrated the scale of the win. "It's remarkably good. I was not expecting such a result," Kulbergs said. Voter turnout was 51.8%, down from 59.4% in 2022, underscoring disappointment with politicians in Latvia, Ikstens said. United List was followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First, which was on 13.1%. Latvia First had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote. Third in the ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.7%, followed by the National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the Kremlin, at 8.9%. Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised more anti-drone capability for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO. His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus on tackling cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country's Russian-speaking minority. Although pro-Russian parties increased their representation, Kits said they remained sidelined and were unlikely to influence government policy. Latvia's ethnic Russian minority is split between those who oppose Moscow's war in Ukraine and others who voice frustration with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life, which many of them see as discriminatory. Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south.

item.title: Haunted by grief, Gaza's displaced still wait overseas for return
item.description: Omar al-Hassayna fled Gaza for Cairo after an Israeli airstrike wiped out much of his large family. Three years on, he remains there waiting for enough stability, security and reconstruction in his still devastated homeland to return.
item.dc:creator: Nidal Al-Mughrabi
item.content:encoded: Omar al-Hassayna fled Gaza for Cairo after an Israeli airstrike wiped out much of his large family. Three years on, he remains there waiting for enough stability, security and reconstruction in his still devastated homeland to return. Hassayna is one of more than 100,000 Gazans who left the enclave during the war that was triggered by the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and who remain stranded overseas, according to Palestinian Authority figures. They still mourn dead relatives and their [USN:L1N45F09E TEXT:"destroyed homes"] and neighbourhoods. "I left Gaza and came to Egypt, the land of Kinana (referring to Egypt), but at the same time, this will not be forgotten, my dear brother, it will not be forgotten," he said. "I am waiting for the opportunity, I am waiting for the moment when Gaza becomes stable so I can return to my country, and be a productive member of this country, and be a positive force for the country." Nearly a year after a ceasefire in Gaza that was meant to start a process of reconstruction under a technocratic government along with a political process that would lead to an eventual full Israeli withdrawal, little has changed. Israeli forces still hold more than 60% of the territory and conduct almost daily airstrikes, while Hamas controls most of the area where Palestinians live, mostly in temporary shelters with what aid agencies call inadequate aid supplies and no prospect of reconstruction soon. Some 308 members of Hassayna's [USN:L8N4400Z0 TEXT:"extended family"] were killed when Israeli strikes destroyed a cluster of Gaza City apartment buildings where they had gathered for shelter on November 22, 2023, according to Palestinian authorities. Among those killed were his wife, four of their adult sons and four small grandchildren including an infant only a few months old. Hassayna's oldest son Mohammed is also in Cairo along with his own four children, as is the widow of one of his dead sons with her daughter. He has brothers in the Egyptian capital too. One daughter was medically evacuated to Turkey with her husband and six children, and another daughter remains in Gaza with her five children although her husband was killed in the attack. The Israeli military did not respond to a request for comment on the details of the November 22 strike. It said its attacks in Gaza are directed at military targets, while trying to reduce harm to civilians. ABOUT 7,000 PALESTINIANS HAVE RETURNED TO GAZA In August, Hassayna watched on video from Cairo as relatives buried 112 family members, including his wife, sons and grandchildren, whose bodies had been recovered from the rubble, with dozens still missing. Hassayna owned a business selling tools for firefighting and safety equipment in Gaza and some of his goods survived the war. He periodically sells some to fund his stay in Cairo, where he has remarried. All those who left Gaza were vetted before their departure by both Israel and Egypt, but many have found it hard to return to the territory. Although some Israeli politicians have urged a policy of encouraging all Gaza's population to leave and to prevent those who left from returning, about 7,000 have gone home. Hassayna believes Egypt will stop any widespread displacement of Palestinians from Gaza. However, no widespread return of those who fled Gaza may be likely until the territory's prospects are clearer. "If Gaza returns. If there is an international agreement (with) a comprehensive situation for the Palestinian people and construction begins, why would I delay?" he said.

item.title: Revolut's rise to become Europe's $115 billion big bank rival
item.description: Revolut has become Europe's most valuable startup and a challenge to centuries-old banking giants, though it faces hurdles.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence White, Elizabeth Howcroft
item.content:encoded: Revolut has risen to become Europe's most valuable startup and a challenge to centuries-old banking giants, having grown rapidly since it was launched just over a decade ago as a fintech promising cheaper forex fees. Yet Revolut faces many hurdles itself, with the amount of revenue it extracts per customer a fraction of its established competitors and a small lending business by industry standards. A spokesperson for Revolut said in an email that the London-based company has a "diversified business model", earning its revenue from various products and services rather than lending. "That means our growth depends on building things customers value, rather than on interest rates," the spokesperson said. Here's Revolut's rise, in five charts: GOING FOR GLOBAL CEO Nik Storonsky has stressed he wants Revolut to be truly global, expanding into markets [USN:L4N44E0AO TEXT:"from Mexico to Australia"]. The company has announced several new licences in recent weeks, as it aims to become one of only a handful of banks with retail operations spanning so much of the globe. Meanwhile, some traditional lenders seen as global, including HSBC (HSBA.L) , are reducing their retail footprint. Valued at $115 billion privately, Revolut is now worth more than Britain's Barclays (BARC.L) and France's Societe Generale (SOGN.PA) as investors bet on its tech platform winning over more customers globally. Revolut's 2025 pretax profit was £1.7 billion ($2.2 billion), a fraction of Barclays' £9 billion, but growing fast. Paulo Macedo, CEO of Portugal's biggest bank, Caixa Geral de Depósitos, said in June that 2025 was the last year in which the 150-year-old bank would record higher profit than Revolut. "When you go to Europe the bank CEOs there are talking about Revolut as their most important threat because of their aggressive marketing and growth," said Cihan Duran, director at S&P Global Ratings. MARRED BY SETBACKS In the US, where Revolut has a provisional license, it will face tougher competition, investors said. "The US could be potentially the biggest growth for Revolut. But at the same time, the US is the most competitive market," said Konstantin Sidorov, CEO of the London Technology Club, which invested in Revolut when it was valued at just $5.5 billion. There have been setbacks, including a fine in Lithuania for failing to prevent money laundering. Revolut said an investigation had not identified any confirmed instances of money laundering, adding that it had signed a settlement with the central bank and taken steps to resolve shortcomings. And in September, Revolut accidentally sent customer data to hackers posing as government investigators. The company said its systems and customer funds were unaffected and it had contacted the "limited number of impacted individuals" to give support. In 2024 and 2025, Revolut was the most-complained-about bank in Britain in fraud cases whereby customers are tricked into sending cash to scammers, Ombudsman data compiled by consumer advocacy firm Which? showed. Revolut has previously said in response it takes fraud very seriously and has robust customer protections in place. CUSTOMERS HAVE SURGED A striking measure of its growth is customer numbers. In Ireland, for example, Revolut said that 80% of the adult population has a Revolut account. Revolut's website shows it has 80 million customers, against 84 million for JPMorgan (JPM.N) and 41 million for HSBC. REVENUE-PER-CUSTOMER IS LOW Revolut makes far less from each of its customers than traditional banks, a Reuters analysis of its figures shows. Average deposit balances are also much lower. Lower per-customer revenue is in part because Revolut lends much less than traditional banks, instead relying on fees such as card subscriptions. With just £2.2 billion in loans at end-2025, Revolut's loan-to-deposit ratio of 6% compares with 55% for HSBC and 86% for Societe Generale. Scaling its lending business will introduce risks including managing big and complex credit exposures, while entering fiercely competitive local mortgage markets will not be easy, analysts and investors said. TOO FEW PRIMARY ACCOUNTS Revolut has attracted customers with its easy-to-use app but executives acknowledge too few use it as a primary bank account. Revolut declined to comment in its latest results on how many customers did so in 2025, but said the figure was up 45% from a year ago. This metric is a focus for Revolut's biggest backers. Alex Immerman, an investor at Andreessen Horowitz, which is known as "a16z", told Reuters it was watching for primary-account adoption, as well as total customer balances. ($1 = 0.7573 pounds)

item.title: Leftist and nationalists lead in election for Bosnia's tripartite presidency
item.description: Voters are casting ballots for the central tripartite presidency and national parliament.
item.dc:creator: Branko Filipovic, Fedja Grulovic
item.content:encoded: A Bosniak left-leaning moderate, a pro-Russian Serb nationalist and a Croatian nationalist are leading Sunday's election for Bosnia's inter-ethnic tripartite presidency, the election commission said, based on ballots from more than 90% of polling stations. The results were largely in line with expectations and with projections by the Poliwave tracking platform, although voter turnout was low at a combined 42.2% in Bosnia's two entities, the Bosniak-Croat Federation and the Serb Republika Srpska. Voters also cast ballots for the national parliament, alongside regional races in the two entities. Voter frustration has grown over an economic slowdown, the slow pace of EU entry talks and a lingering political crisis in which ethnically based dominant parties from the two entities have repeatedly stalled decisions by the weak central government that links them. Denis Becirovic, a Bosniak of the Social Democratic Party (SDP-BiH) and part of the current tripartite presidency, garnered 26.66% of votes in the Bosniak-Croat Federation, ahead of the candidate for the centrist and traditionalist Bosniak Muslim Party of Democratic Action (SDA). The two had been considered close favourites in the election. Also leading in the Bosniak-Croat Federation was newcomer Darijana Filipovic of the nationalist and pro-European Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ-BiH), with 14% of the vote. In Republika Srpska, Zeljka Cvijanovic, an existing member of the tripartite presidency from the Serb and pro-Russian nationalist Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), secured 55.34% of votes, the election commission said. Voting continued in some polling stations after the 7 p.m. (1700 GMT) deadline due to delays related to a new electronic balloting system, Bosnia's Central Election Commission head Jovan Kalaba told reporters in Sarajevo. The election commission redesigned ballots and introduced new biometric voter identification and electronic scanners, which it said were aimed at curbing voting fraud. Speaking in Banja Luka, the largest Bosnian Serb city, Milorad Dodik, a separatist and pro-Russian leader of the SNSD who visited Moscow and met Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, said his party's candidate Savo Minic won the most votes for president of the Republika Srpska entity. "We have won the member of the (Bosnian) Presidency, and the president of the Republika Srpska. An unexpectedly high result," Dodik said. Since the Bosnian war ended in 1995 under the US-brokered Dayton peace accord, the country has been split along ethnic lines into two entities linked by the weak central government and tripartite presidency. Bosnia, which has struggled to recover from the 1992-95 war, secured EU candidate status in December 2022 and approval to open accession negotiations in 2024. Actual talks have not started, however, because the domestic legislatures have yet to enact core requirements such as bolstering judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption laws. Borjana Kristo, the deputy-head of the Croat HDZ-BiH, said that overall progress could be made through dialogue after the elections. "Bosnia must make progress solely on the principle of consensus, dialogue, and mutual respect," she told party supporters, cautioning against rhetoric that would drag the country backwards. Many voters in the country of 3.4 million people say they want to move beyond divisive rhetoric but its politics have become deadlocked. The EU and Russia have been vying for influence over Bosnia, with the EU seeking to expand its membership across the Balkans while Russia wants to slow that process down and preserve its influence over the Republika Srpska. The US has also sought to bolster its influence in Bosnia, pushing for a $1.5 billion [USN:L6N40Y0SF TEXT:"pipeline project"] to import US liquefied natural gas. The EU has said, however, that the selection of the company for the project lacked competitive transparency, while Washington and Brussels have also clashed over the role of the [USN:L6N41N07W TEXT:"High Representative"], the international peace overseer for the country.

item.title: Merz unveils fresh military aid in Kyiv, says Germany won't be intimidated
item.description: Germany's chancellor said Moscow was trying to break the morale of the Ukrainian people, and announced €350 million for repairs in the energy sector.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Rinke, Felix Hoske
item.content:encoded: Germany will not be intimidated into dropping its support for Ukraine, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Sunday as he announced a further €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in military aid during a visit to Kyiv marked by Russian drone attacks. Air-raid sirens and explosions rang out repeatedly across the Ukrainian capital as Merz and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy visited a memorial to soldiers killed during the four-year-old war, as well as the [USN:L1N45K0A2 TEXT:"Academy of Sciences"], where at least two people died in a drone strike last week. Russia has escalated its drone attacks on Kyiv and other cities in recent weeks, targeting telecoms, electricity and transport infrastructure as well as military assets. Speaking at a press conference alongside Zelenskiy, Merz said Moscow was trying to break the morale of the Ukrainian people, and announced €350 million for repairs in the energy sector. He said Germany remained Ukraine's strongest backer. DEALS WITH GERMAN COMPANIES WORTH €6.6 BILLION "We do this not only to protect Ukraine's territorial integrity; we do it deeply in our own interest, for it is a matter of Europe's security," Merz said, noting that Russia was carrying out cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns that struck at Europe's democratic order. "This demonstrates that we will not be intimidated," he said. Russia has said accusations of hybrid warfare are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria. German officials said executives from companies, who travelled with Merz, had signed 14 agreements with the Ukrainian government and businesses worth roughly €6.6 billion. Among those deals, Ukraine inked an agreement with Germany's Diehl Defence for the supply of IRIS-T air defence missiles, as well as a deal for radar equipment with Hensoldt and for jet drone interceptors with Quantum Systems. "What is important in this visit is that not only Germany is helping Ukraine, but Ukraine is sharing its knowledge, experience, as well as orders," Zelenskiy said. "These are jobs for Germany." Zelenskiy praised a new jet drone interceptor, dubbed SPYS and developed by Quantum, for showing promising results. He said Ukraine and Germany were close to [USN:L1N44U0N8 TEXT:"finalising a broad defence deal"], which he has previously said would include the production of drones, missiles and related software. ZELENSKIY VOWS TO RESPOND Since the summer, Russia has targeted civilian and military infrastructure daily with dozens of high-speed jet-powered [USN:L8N4521KI TEXT:"attack drones"] – which Ukraine has struggled to down because they are much faster than previous propeller versions. One of the Russian strikes on Sunday hit the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, damaging its roadway, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. The explosion injured two people and damaged a hot water supply system in the area, he said. Zelenskiy said Russia's decision to escalate air strikes against infrastructure targets was due to setbacks it had suffered on the battlefield, and he vowed that Ukraine would retaliate. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin wanted to force residents to flee Ukraine's major cities. "If our bridges collapse, we will manage to get out of this situation, but his people will feel it too ... This is maximum escalation of this war," Zelenskiy told reporters. Russia has been [USN:L1N45P00Z TEXT:"attacking"] Kyiv's bridges since last week in an effort to disrupt links between the capital's two sides and logistics routes between central and eastern Ukraine. MERZ APPEALS FOR END TO 'SENSELESS WAR' Zelenskiy said US peace envoy Steve Witkoff has messaged him to urge a return to trilateral talks as soon as possible. He said Ukraine was willing to meet this month and hoped Russia would join, but he said Western allies needed to apply more pressure to Moscow to bring the war to an end. Earlier in the day, during the visit to the badly damaged Academy of Sciences, Merz appealed to Putin to "put an end to this senseless war". "We are ready for talks, we are ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop," the German leader said. Russia's Foreign Ministry [USN:L1N45P03K TEXT:"said"] on Saturday that Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in Ukraine in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia. It warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against travelling to Ukraine. ($1 = 0.8887 euros)

item.title: Cornell president vows 'serious look' at fraternities, sororities in wake of rape allegations
item.description: Michael Kotlikoff said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the future.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus following an outcry over the school's handling of a student's rape allegations, the Ivy League school's president said on Saturday. A [USN:L1N45O0OO TEXT:"civil lawsuit"] filed last month by the woman, who alleges she was drugged and raped in 2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has sparked [USN:L6N45O0CP TEXT:"outrage and soul-searching"] at Cornell over its campus culture at the school in Ithaca, New York. In a video message, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the future. That includes "a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life," Kotlikoff said. "At their best, these organizations can provide students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a powerful sense of community," he said. "But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility." The university will seek input, he said, from students, alumni and others on how to "preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and well-being of others." The lawsuit against Cornell, seven fraternity members and others, alleges that the school failed to adequately punish some of the accused students. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times reported. Cornell has defended its handling of the matter, saying it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity from campus. The school said it imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions. But "we must do better," Kotlikoff said. "We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves." He vowed that university officials would "be more transparent" about their actions related to the 2024 incident, but he did not detail specific initiatives that the university would take. "In the coming weeks, we will create additional opportunities for members of our community to ask questions and hear directly from university leadership," he said. The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.

item.title: LE POINT sur les élections au Brésil
item.description: Quelque 160 millions d'électeurs brésiliens sont appelés aux urnes dimanche à l'occasion du premier tour de l'élection présidentielle, un scrutin décisif pour le plus grand pays d'Amérique du Sud qui déterminera s'il emprunte à son tour le virage ultra-conservateur observé sur le continent.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Quelque 160 millions d'électeurs brésiliens sont appelés aux urnes dimanche à l'occasion du premier tour de l'élection présidentielle, un scrutin décisif pour le plus grand pays d'Amérique du Sud qui déterminera s'il emprunte à son tour le virage ultra-conservateur observé sur le continent. Selon les sondages, le président sortant de gauche Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, qui brigue à 80 ans un quatrième mandat non consécutif, est au coude-à-coude avec le sénateur de droite Flavio Bolsonaro, 45 ans, fils de l'ex-président Jair Bolsonaro condamné à 27 ans de prison pour tentative de coup d'Etat. Treize candidats au total sont en lice pour accéder au palais du Planalto, dans un scrutin où le vote est obligatoire pour les Brésiliens âgés de 18 à 70 ans. Un second tour sera organisé le 25 octobre si aucun candidat n'emporte la majorité absolue dimanche. Outre l'élection présidentielle se tiennent également les 4 et 25 octobre les élections parlementaires visant à renouveler les 513 sièges de la Chambre des députés et un tiers des 81 sièges du Sénat composant le Congrès national. Les électeurs doivent également désigner les gouverneurs des 26 États fédérés et renouveler les assemblées législatives de ces derniers. Voici les principaux développements et éléments à savoir: * Les Brésiliens se rendent aux urnes dans un contexte de forte polarisation [USN:L6N45Q03K] * Brésil-Lula et Flavio Bolsonaro clôturent leurs campagnes avant le premier tour des élections [USN:L6N45P07U] * AVANT-PAPIER-Brésil-Lula et Bolsonaro au coude-à-coude pour la présidence [USN:L6N45N0MU] * PORTRAIT-Brésil-Flavio Bolsonaro, la présidentielle en héritage [USN:L6N45L0NC] * PORTRAIT-Lula porte les espoirs de la gauche, au-delà du Brésil [USN:L8N45L137] * ENCADRÉ-Brésil-Dans la course à la présidence, les écueils budgétaires sont passés sous silence [USN:L6N45L0SH]

item.title: Brazil's Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro wrap up campaigns ahead of first-round vote
item.description: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday ahead of Sunday's first-round presidential election, each expressing confidence of victory despite polls pointing to a likely runoff.
item.dc:creator: Lisandra Paraguassu, Sebastian Rocandio
item.content:encoded: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday ahead of Sunday's first-round [USN:L6N45K0PD TEXT:"presidential election"], each expressing confidence of victory despite polls pointing to a [USN:S0N45F00D TEXT:"likely runoff"]. [USN:L6N45K0PD TEXT:"Lula"] ended his re-election campaign with a march through Sao Paulo that drew large crowds of supporters, while [USN:L1N45F0NC TEXT:"Bolsonaro"] took part in a motorcycle caravan through Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana in Sao Paulo state and later rallied in Rio de Janeiro. Lula's camp hailed the event as a record turnout, larger than the closing rally of his 2022 campaign. Organizers said some 150,000 supporters filled the two-kilometer stretch of Augusta Street between Paulista Avenue and Roosevelt Square, a traditional stage for political demonstrations in Brazil's largest city. Speaking from a campaign vehicle, Lula called Sunday's election a choice between "democracy and barbarism." The head of the leftist leader's Workers' Party, Edinho Silva, said the turnout reflected growing momentum for Lula. "Unlike other Latin American countries, where we saw a right-wing wave at the end, here in Brazil we're seeing a wave in our favor," Silva said. Right-wing Senator Bolsonaro urged supporters to turn out to vote and predicted a first-round win. "I am convinced that everything is in place for us to win this election in the first round," the lawmaker said. Flavio was photographed holding a placard bearing the image of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest after being convicted of attempting to overturn the 2022 election result, which he lost to Lula. If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes -- which exclude blank and null ballots -- in Sunday's first-round vote, the two frontrunners advance to a second-round runoff on October 25.

item.title: OpenAI safety employee quits, says 'time for trial and error is over'
item.description: AI companies are not being "nearly careful enough," David Robinson wrote in the Atlantic.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A former OpenAI safety employee who recently resigned criticized the company's approach to AI safety, arguing that a fast-paced culture focused on rapid development increases the risk of failures. Writing in "I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken," published by the Atlantic on Saturday, David Robinson said AI companies, including OpenAI, were not being "nearly careful enough" and should place greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems. "The time for trial and error is over," Robinson wrote, arguing that advanced AI systems require safeguards more akin to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation. Robinson said OpenAI relies heavily on what it calls "iterative deployment," releasing systems and strengthening safeguards when problems emerge. The comments add to a [USN:L6N45L0PN TEXT:"debate within the AI industry"] over whether companies are moving too quickly to develop increasingly powerful systems. [USN:L4N45L05X TEXT:"OpenAI"] and rival [USN:L6N45L00I TEXT:"Anthropic"] have faced scrutiny after incidents in which safety controls failed, or experimental systems behaved unexpectedly. Robinson, who said he spent 3-1/2 years at OpenAI, helped draft the company's preparedness framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, wrote: "As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed." "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement. Robinson also warned that AI capabilities were advancing faster than researchers' understanding of alignment, a field focused on ensuring AI systems act in accordance with human goals and values.
