item.title: Latvia PM Kulbergs wins election held under shadow of Ukraine war
item.description: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centrist, pro-Ukraine United List party won Saturday's parliamentary election by an unexpectedly wide margin, partial results showed, with many voters on edge amid warnings of potential Russian aggression.
item.dc:creator: Andrius Sytas, Terje Solsvik
item.content:encoded: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centrist, pro-Ukraine United List party won Saturday's parliamentary election by an unexpectedly wide margin, partial results showed, with many voters on edge amid warnings of potential Russian aggression. With 88% of ballots counted, United List was on 36.6%, followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First on 13.4%. Latvia First had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote. Baltic countries have warned for months that Russia is mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine and sow fear, although Western officials dismiss concerns that Moscow is capable of launching a direct assault on NATO, of which Latvia is a member. Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria. Reacting to exit poll readings earlier in the evening, Kulbergs said he hoped to remain prime minister but that he would not want to govern with Latvia First. According to partial results, he will still need coalition allies to form a government. "It's remarkably good. I was not expecting such a result," Kulbergs said at his party's headquarters in Riga. Third in the exit poll ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.6%, followed by the nationalist National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the Kremlin, at 9.1%. SHADOW OF UKRAINE WAR A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which [USN:L1N41K03T TEXT:"stray military drones flew"] undetected into Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials [USN:L8N41X1AC TEXT:"have blamed Russia"] for causing them to divert from their flight paths. "The priority, in my view, is, of course, security – security in Latvia," said Megija Nordena, 21, from Riga. "And then ... as a student, I’d say support for students, the economy, and also support for pensioners." Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs has also promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO. His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and should instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country's Russian-speaking minority. "Our voters want peace, to stop looking for shelters, to no longer experience the air alerts," Sovereign Power party leader Julia Stepanenko told Reuters. "The war must not be encouraged in any way, including by financing it ... Ukraine must win, but through peace talks." The ethnic Russian minority in Latvia is split between those who feel embarrassed or angry about the Kremlin's war in Ukraine, and those frustrated with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life that many see as discriminatory. Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea, and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south.

item.title: How Brazil's election winner could reshape its institutions as vacancies mount
item.description: The next president will inherit a large number of appointments to Brazil's most powerful institutions.
item.dc:creator: Marcela Ayres, Ricardo Brito
item.content:encoded: Brazil's next president is set to inherit an unusually large number of appointments to the country's most powerful institutions, with vacancies piled up at the Supreme Court, central bank and economic regulators. The growing backlog of unfilled posts means the winner of the [USN:L6N45K0PD TEXT:"tight race"] between leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro could gain significant influence over bodies that help shape monetary policy, oversee financial markets and interpret the constitution. The two candidates will face off in the first round of the electoral contest on Sunday, with a runoff later in the month forecast as the most likely outcome. The vacancies reflect a broader shift in Brazilian politics: an increasingly powerful Congress is using confirmation of nominees as a tool for political leverage, eroding the executive branch's room for maneuver. A predominantly right-wing Congress has flexed this growing power during Lula's current term by delaying confirmation of a number of his nominees. Lula has also failed to make some nominations. While nominations once went promptly to Senate committees for approval, many nomination processes stalled during the pandemic, awaiting the Senate president's approval. Senate President Davi Alcolumbre has maintained that practice, concentrating power in the Senate and turning what was once a routine step into a political decision, said a person familiar with the process, who requested anonymity. The presidential palace and Alcolumbre's office did not respond to requests for comment. The use of presidential appointments as political leverage has made the executive reluctant to submit nominees without first gauging their Senate prospects, said Rubens Beçak, a law professor at the University of Sao Paulo. BANK SEATS At the central bank, two board seats, including the economic policy post that oversees forecasts ahead of rate decisions, have been empty since January, a record length of time for those posts to be left open. Lula has yet to submit nominees. In April, senators [USN:S0N41A02V TEXT:"rejected Lula's Supreme Court nominee"], Solicitor General Jorge Messias, in a historic setback that extended a vacancy now nearly a year old, the longest since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s. Securities regulator CVM has had board vacancies since late 2024, while antitrust watchdog Cade, lacking its president and two board members, is near its minimum quorum, delaying merger reviews. Claudio Couto, a political scientist at the Fundacao Getulio Vargas, called the backlog "deeply problematic," saying it risks concentrating appointments in one administration and politicizing "bodies that are meant to remain nonpartisan." STRUCTURAL SHIFT Nominations and bills, once largely negotiated between the president and coalition parties, increasingly hinge on deals among congressional leaders, said Neuriberg Dias, head of legislative watchdog DIAP. Congress' growing control over spending, he said, has changed the incentives behind executive-legislative bargaining. Congressional earmarks — which direct funding to local or pet projects — accounted for 7.5% of effective federal discretionary spending in 2018, but swelled to 21% in 2025, according to Planning Ministry data provided to Reuters. The government's grip on the agenda has in turn weakened. Last year, Congress approved 178 bills introduced by legislators and only 50 from the executive. In 2007, during Lula's second term, the reverse was true: 142 executive bills versus 52 from Congress, according to DIAP data. The 2026 campaign has slowed nominations further, people familiar with the matter said, as lawmakers wait to see whether Lula wins another term. Voters will also elect all 513 members of the Lower House and two-thirds of the Senate. With power shifting from the presidency to Congress, the election may decide not only who governs Brazil, but how much room the winner will have to appoint officials and shape key institutions.

item.title: $5 billion Firmus IPO divides investors after valuation triples in two months
item.description: As Australian data centre operator Firmus prepares to launch a $5 billion initial public offering, the country's second-largest ever, prospective investors are questioning the firm's surging valuation, citing an "unproven" track record.
item.dc:creator: Christine Chen
item.content:encoded: As Australian data centre operator Firmus prepares to launch a $5 billion initial public offering, the country's second-largest ever, prospective investors are questioning the firm's surging valuation, citing an "unproven" track record. Firmus [USN:L1N45N0G2 TEXT:"on Thursday"] priced its shares at A$11 ($7.63) each, giving the company an equity valuation of $30.6 billion, according to a term sheet seen by Reuters. That's nearly triple the $10.5 billion valuation it achieved following a [USN:L4N444084 TEXT:"fundraising round"] at the start of August. The leap in valuation in less than two months has prompted some investors to scrutinize whether the company, which is backed by Blackstone, Nvidia (NVDA.O) and local firms including Wilson Asset Management (WAA.AX) and Argo (ARG.AX) , can deliver on its ambitious growth projections. Firmus estimates that five planned data centres across Asia-Pacific, together with its existing facilities in Melbourne and Singapore, will generate some $5 billion in annual earnings within five years, Reuters [USN:L4N45F0GG TEXT:"reported"] last month. "Our process prevents us from effectively buying into, kind of, the hopes and dreams," said Merlon Capital Partners portfolio manager Kirit Hara. "We're anchored towards what's actually on the table. And what's on the table in terms of operating and development, we're struggling to get to that kind of A$40-odd billion dollar market cap." The company's $30 billion worth of debt was also a concern given rising costs and interest rates, Hara added. Firmus declined to comment for this report. Indicative orders from potential investors for the IPO are already above the deal's size, the term sheet said. Bookbuilding will begin on Tuesday and the stock is due to start trading on the Australian Securities Exchange on October 23. Morningstar strategist Lochlan Halloway said in a note that Firmus had hallmarks of a "boom phase", pointing to the "wild increase in valuation in such a short period of time." Its debt pile is around six times its forecast earnings, Halloway added. Katana Asset Management portfolio manager Romano Sala Tenna said Firmus' IPO prospects were polarising potential investors, and he was still undecided on whether to participate. "We are struggling with the fundamental arithmetic, and that there is an enormous amount of execution which is required to justify the valuation," Sala Tenna said. Firmus did not meet the firm's investment criteria such as cash flow and earnings, but could be attractive as a trade if passive funds participate and create strong demand for the shares after listing, he said. Sydney's Blackwattle Investment Partners would not be bidding for Firmus stock, said portfolio manager Joseph Koh. "Because we don't have enough confidence in the delivery of the future projects, we can't get any confidence on the valuation that underpins that," Koh said. Blackwattle prefers exposure to the AI theme through companies like Goodman Group (GMG.AX) , which Koh said had a better track record of developing data centres on time and on budget compared to "unproven" Firmus. "There are so many unknowns," he said about Firmus. "But that doesn't mean we would look to short it either." ($1 = 1.4413 Australian dollars)

item.title: How one millennial is building wealth by buying assets, not stuff
item.description: Some are figuring out how to turn reselling into a source of income.
item.dc:creator: Hani Richter
item.content:encoded: Dandan Zhu. Courtesy Dandan Zhu/Handout via REUTERS When Dandan Zhu purchased a Rolex in 2012 for $2,400, she didn’t just treat it like a luxury watch —she saw it as an asset. Years later, that investment paid off. When her tenants failed to pay rent on time, Zhu sold the Rolex and broke even, giving her a quick influx of cash to cover her mortgage. “I deeply understand retail arbitrage,” the New York-based 38-year-old says, referring to the practice of reselling goods for a profit. As a university student, she sold gaming consoles on eBay to help pay off her tuition. Even after graduating in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and landing her first job in recruitment, she continued buying and reselling goods to supplement her income, eventually climbing the career ladder and purchasing her first home in 2014. Nowadays, the former headhunter-turned-content creator trades primarily in limited-edition luxury bags that she knows will retain value and, if needed, generate income. “I specifically know specific products I can guarantee a $2,000 profit,” she says, noting that while basic bags will depreciate in value, "the ones that will appreciate are those (that are) very special.” Dandan Zhu. Courtesy Dandan Zhu/Handout via REUTERS While she researches products online and in-store, Zhu says she also relies on AI to help her identify which items are likely to appreciate in value in the longterm. THE WIDER TREND A 2026 ThredUp and GlobalData Resale Report found that more than half of Gen Z and millennial consumers browse or prioritize second-hand purchases before buying new. Cory Christiana, a Boston-based certified financial planner and investment adviser at NEXTEN FP, sees this trend as generational. “Each generation sees what the generation did before and tends to set their own path,” he says, noting that while boomers accumulated homes and financial assets, younger generations, facing affordability challenges and lives increasingly lived online, may be drawn towards more physical assets. “It’s important to slow down and ask yourself if there is real value in a purchase or if it's something you want,” he says. “The distinction is an important one.” Historically, certain jewelry, collectible cars, and artwork have retained and grown in value over time. But Christiana emphasizes that these kinds of assets work best as additions to a diversified portfolio — including stocks, bonds, real estate and cash — rather than as a replacement for them. KEY TAKEAWAYS A luxury item can function as emergency liquidity. When Zhu's tenants stopped paying rent and she had little working capital, the Rolex she sold gave her something she could convert into cash when she needed it. Research before buying. Check realistic resale prices and total transaction costs before treating a purchase as an asset. It’s important to note that an item only qualifies as an asset if it is rare and other people are willing to pay for it. A limited-edition watch or handbag fits this criterion; mass-produced goods for fast fashion, however, typically do not. Investing in assets works well within a diverse financial plan. Treat resalable assets as an addition to a wider portfolio of investments, not a replacement. Have a money lesson or story to share? Tell us what worked for you — or what didn’t — by emailing hani.richter@tr.com .
